title: Personality in Perspective
overview: After surveying nearly two dozen theories, from Freud at the start of the 20th century to 21st-century research, the closing chapter asks which theory is correct and answers that none holds the whole truth: each theorist supplied a piece of the puzzle. The chapter pulls those pieces together into seven broad factors that shape personality: genetic, environmental, learning, parental, developmental, consciousness and unconscious. For each factor it shows where the theorists agree, where they differ, and what recent research says. Heredity supplies predispositions rather than destinies; environment (family position, culture, generation, jobs, life events, ethnicity, region and neighbourhood) works mainly through learning; parents matter, though the peer-influence controversy and genetic research challenge how much; personality keeps changing beyond childhood while basic traits stabilise around age 30; consciousness is accepted almost universally; and the unconscious, now studied as a rational non-conscious, remains the least understood factor. The chapter closes by stressing that the question 'What is personality?' is still open and is really the attempt to understand ourselves.
objectives: Explain why the chapter treats the many personality theories as complementary pieces of one puzzle rather than as rival, competing answers.
Summarise the evidence for a genetic factor in personality and explain why inherited traits are predispositions rather than destinies.

Compare how Adler, Horney, Allport, Cattell, Erikson, Maslow and Rogers acknowledged the social environment, and describe research on generation, parenthood, jobs, life events, ethnicity, culture, region and neighbourhood.
Describe how learning (Skinner, Bandura, Rotter, Seligman) transmits environmental influence and why control is a learned dimension of personality.
Compare theorists' views on the parental factor, distinguish authoritative from authoritarian parenting, and evaluate the parents-versus-peers controversy and the kibbutz and day-care evidence.
Evaluate whether personality is fixed in childhood or changes across the life span, using research on stability after age 30 and McAdams' three levels of personality.
Compare how theorists treat conscious processes, and contrast Freud's emotional unconscious with the modern rational non-conscious.
Write comparative exam answers that integrate several theorists around a single factor.

sections.heading: Personality in Perspective: Pieces of the Puzzle
sections.detailed:
The final chapter returns to the purpose set out in Chapter 1: to explore the forces that make us who we are. Having covered nearly two dozen theories, from Sigmund Freud's work around 1900 to developments in the 21st century, the authors admit that a student could easily conclude that the field is more chaos than certainty, more disagreement than agreement.

The authors pose the obvious question: which theory is right, and which one solves the puzzle of personality? Their answer is that no single theory wins. Each theory describes factors that influence personality to some degree, and each theorist contributed an essential piece of the puzzle. The task of this chapter is to lay those pieces side by side so that a fuller picture can emerge.

To do this, the chapter does not go theory by theory. Instead it reorganises the whole book around seven broad themes or factors that cut across the theories: the genetic factor, the environmental factor, the learning factor, the parental factor, the developmental factor, the consciousness factor and the unconscious factor. Under each factor it shows which theorists emphasised it, how far they agree, and what research has found. A short final comment then reflects on the state of the field.

This structure is important for exams. Questions on this chapter are usually comparative: they ask how different theorists view heredity, childhood, parents, change, or awareness. The best answers therefore name several theorists under each factor and show both agreement and disagreement, rather than retelling one theory in isolation.
sections.simple: With so many theories, it can look like psychologists cannot agree on anything. The authors say every theory got part of the answer right. This chapter groups the theories under seven factors that shape personality so we can see the whole picture.
keyPoints: Nearly two dozen theories were covered, from Freud to 21st-century research.
No single theory is 'correct'; each supplies a vital piece of the puzzle.
The chapter organises the field around seven factors: genetic, environmental, learning, parental, developmental, consciousness and unconscious.
Exam answers on this chapter should compare several theorists under each factor.

sections.heading: The Genetic Factor
sections.detailed:
Evidence is growing stronger that many personality traits or dimensions are inherited. The chapter lists several trait systems with a genetic basis: Eysenck's three dimensions of psychoticism, neuroticism and extraversion (extraversion being derived from Jung's work); McCrae and Costa's five-factor model of neuroticism, extraversion, openness to experience, agreeableness and conscientiousness; and Buss and Plomin's three temperaments of emotionality, activity and sociability. Zuckerman's trait of sensation seeking is also described as mainly genetic. For this reason the trait approach, with its focus on heredity, remains a necessary and useful research area.

What is still unresolved is how many inherited factors there really are. Is the right number Cattell's sixteen, Eysenck's three, McCrae and Costa's five, Buss and Plomin's three, or some number not yet discovered? This is a clear point of disagreement among trait theorists even though they agree on heredity itself.

Research support is wide. Twin studies from Canada, Germany and Japan supported a genetic basis for the five-factor model, and the lead author (Yamagata) suggested it may reflect a heritage shared by the whole human species. The Big Five were found to become increasingly stable over 20 years from childhood to adulthood (Shiner). Twin and sibling studies in Germany and Belgium found high trait stability across childhood, adolescence and young adulthood (DeFruyt and colleagues; Kandler and colleagues). A programme covering 50 cultures, such as Israel, Korea and Turkey, found the Big Five in most nations, though less consistently in developing countries such as Ethiopia, Lebanon, Malaysia and Uganda (Allik, Realo and McCrae and others).

Genetics also appears in specific and even everyday characteristics. Swedish adolescent twin research found a strong genetic component in psychopathic personality prone to violent antisocial behaviour (Larsson and colleagues), and the heritability of anxiety rose between ages 14 and 18 (Garcia and colleagues). Studies in the United States, Finland, French-speaking Canada and Sweden found genetic influences on sexual attitudes, eating behaviour in 2-year-olds, depression in bullied children, and attitudes toward practising a musical instrument; identical twins were also more likely than fraternal twins to own guns. The authors expect behaviour genetics to reveal still more inherited facets.

The key limitation, however, is that not even the strongest supporter of genetics claims heredity explains personality completely. We inherit predispositions, not destinies; tendencies, not certainties. Whether a predisposition is realised depends on social and environmental conditions, especially in childhood. This idea forms the bridge to the environmental factor.
sections.simple: Many traits, like the Big Five, Eysenck's three dimensions, Buss and Plomin's temperaments and sensation seeking, are partly inherited, and twin studies across many countries back this up. Researchers still disagree about how many inherited traits there are. But genes only give us tendencies; whether they show up depends on our environment, especially in childhood.
keyPoints: Inherited dimensions: Eysenck's P-E-N, McCrae and Costa's Big Five, Buss and Plomin's emotionality, activity and sociability, and Zuckerman's sensation seeking.
Unresolved: how many inherited traits exist (Cattell 16, Eysenck 3, McCrae and Costa 5, Buss and Plomin 3?).
Twin research in many countries supports the genetic basis and stability of the Big Five; the Big Five appear in most of 50 cultures studied.
Genes also influence psychopathy, anxiety and everyday behaviours such as eating, sexual attitudes and gun ownership.
We inherit predispositions, not destinies; their expression depends on environment, especially in childhood.

sections.heading: The Environmental Factor
sections.detailed:
Research suggests that genetic effects matter most in infancy and the earliest years, while environmental effects grow steadily more important as we move from childhood into adulthood, and they keep operating across the whole life (Briley and Tucker-Drob; Kandler).

Every theorist in the book accepted that the social environment shapes personality, which makes this a point of broad agreement. Adler stressed birth order: our position among siblings, the age gaps between them, or having no siblings at all exposes us to different parental and social challenges and so produces different personalities. Horney emphasised culture, noting different kinds of neuroses in her German and American patients, the very different environments of boys and girls, and the way female inferiority grows out of treatment in a male-dominated culture; she suggested that women raised in a matriarchal culture might have higher self-esteem. Even the founders of the trait approach agreed. Allport said genetics provides the raw material but the social environment shapes it into the finished product. Cattell held that heredity matters more for some of his 16 factors than for others, but that environment eventually affects every factor to some degree. Erikson's eight stages are innate, but the environment decides how they are realised, and social and historical forces shape ego identity. Maslow and Rogers saw self-actualization as innate but accepted that the environment could block or promote it.

The chapter then lists many kinds of environmental influence. Large societal events such as wars and recessions narrow life choices and affect identity, while ordinary changes such as parenthood, divorce or a new job can also change personality. Generation matters: Twenge compared more than 50,000 college students and young people from the 1950s and 1980s and found much higher anxiety and neuroticism in the 1980s cohort, attributed to reduced social connectedness (more divorce, fewer births, later marriage, more people living alone).

Parenthood changes adults. Finnish research found that becoming a parent brought more stress and anxiety, lower marital and life satisfaction, and higher emotionality, rising with the number of children (Jokela and colleagues); studies in the United States, England and Turkey found that marital satisfaction fell as the number of children rose (Wendorf and colleagues). Work matters too: New Zealanders tested at 18 and 26 who had satisfying, high-status jobs at 26 showed more positive emotionality and less negative emotionality, suggesting the workplace can affect innate traits (Roberts, Caspi and Moffitt). Stressful life events also count: in a 10-year US study, people high in neuroticism saw such events as negative turning points and became more neurotic, while those high in extraversion saw them as lessons and became more extraverted (Sutin and colleagues).

Ethnicity and minority status shape personality through variables such as sensation seeking, locus of control and need for achievement, and minority members must build an ethnic identity alongside an ego identity; in Canada, those with the strongest ethnic identity had the highest self-esteem and well-being (Usborne and Taylor). Culture matters: individualistic Western cultures score higher on extraversion, sensation seeking and subjective well-being than Eastern cultures. Region matters: in the United States neuroticism is higher in the northeast and southeast, agreeableness in the south, and extraversion higher in the northeast and lower in the west (Rentfrow). Even neighbourhood matters: children in economically disadvantaged neighbourhoods show more maladaptive tendencies, low resiliency and problem behaviours (Hart, Atkins and Matsuba), and in London life satisfaction, agreeableness, conscientiousness and openness differed across neighbourhoods (Jokela and colleagues).

The chapter concludes that the impact of environment cannot be denied, and that its most important route of influence is learning.
sections.simple: Genes matter most early in life, but the environment matters more and more as we grow up. Every theorist agreed the social world shapes us, from Adler's birth order to Horney's culture. Research shows that the generation we grow up in, becoming parents, our jobs, stressful events, ethnicity, culture, region and even neighbourhood all affect personality.
keyPoints: Genetic effects are strongest in infancy; environmental effects increase into adulthood and continue through life.
All theorists accepted environment: Adler (birth order), Horney (culture, gender), Allport (raw material shaped by environment), Cattell, Erikson, Maslow and Rogers.
Twenge: 1980s cohort higher in anxiety and neuroticism than 1950s cohort, linked to lower social connectedness.
Parenthood, jobs and stressful life events change adult personality.
Ethnic identity, Western versus Eastern culture, US region and neighbourhood all relate to personality differences.
Environmental influence works mainly through learning.

sections.heading: The Learning Factor
sections.detailed:
The evidence that learning shapes almost every aspect of behaviour, including personality and even our major life goals (Bleidorn and colleagues), is described as overwhelming. All the social and environmental forces covered in the previous section exert their influence through learning. Learning can even act on inherited tendencies, modifying, disrupting, preventing or allowing them to flourish, which links the learning factor back to the genetic one.

The two theorists most associated with learning are Skinner and Bandura. Skinner showed the role of positive reinforcement, successive approximation, superstitious behaviour and other learning variables in shaping what others call personality; for Skinner, personality was simply an accumulation of learned responses. Bandura added that we learn by watching models (observational learning) and through vicarious reinforcement. Bandura agreed with Skinner that most behaviour is learned and that genetics plays only a limited role, which places both of them at the opposite pole from the trait-genetic theorists.

The chapter then points to several personality variables with scientific evidence that they are learned: self-efficacy (Bandura), locus of control (Rotter), learned helplessness, and optimism versus pessimism (Seligman). Although they come from different theorists, these concepts converge on a broader idea, the level of control. People who believe they control their lives are high in self-efficacy, have an internal locus of control, and do not show learned helplessness, which is essentially a lack of control. In Seligman's language, people who feel in control are optimists rather than pessimists. This is a good example of different theories agreeing under different names.

Control is beneficial in many areas. A high degree of control has been linked to better coping, fewer effects of stress, better mental and physical health, perseverance, higher aspirations and self-esteem, lower anxiety, higher grades, and greater social skill and popularity.

Whatever it is called, control is determined by social and environmental factors. It is learned in infancy and childhood, though it can change later in life, and specific parental behaviours help a child feel in control. Control is therefore one of several learned dimensions of personality in which parental behaviour is paramount, which leads into the parental factor.
sections.simple: All environmental influences work through learning, and learning can even change how inherited traits show up. Skinner saw personality as learned responses, and Bandura added learning by watching others. Self-efficacy, locus of control, learned helplessness and optimism all boil down to a sense of control, which is learned in childhood, mainly from parents, and brings many benefits.
keyPoints: Learning is the route through which environmental forces shape personality and can modify inherited tendencies.
Skinner: personality is an accumulation of learned responses shaped by reinforcement, successive approximation and superstitious behaviour.
Bandura: observational learning and vicarious reinforcement; agreed with Skinner that genetics plays a limited role.
Self-efficacy, internal locus of control, absence of learned helplessness and optimism all reflect a learned sense of control.
High control is linked to better coping, health, self-esteem, grades and social skills; it is learned early, largely through parental behaviour.

sections.heading: The Parental Factor: Theorists and Parenting Styles
sections.detailed:
Freud was the first theorist to stress the influence of parents on personality, and almost every later theorist echoed him to some degree, making this one of the strongest areas of agreement in the book. Adler focused on children who feel unwanted or rejected by their parents; such rejection can leave a person insecure, angry and low in self-esteem. Horney, drawing on her own experience, described how a lack of parental warmth and affection undermines a child's security and produces feelings of helplessness.

Even the trait theorists recognised the parental factor. Allport saw the infant's relationship with the mother as the main source of affection and security, which are crucial for later development. Cattell regarded infancy as the major formative period, with parents and siblings shaping the child's character. Erikson held that the relationship with the mother in the first year is vital for developing trust. Maslow stressed that parents must satisfy the child's physiological and safety needs in the first two years, a prerequisite for higher needs to emerge. Rogers emphasised the parents' responsibility to provide unconditional positive regard.

The book has also shown how parental behaviour can build or undermine specific characteristics such as self-efficacy, locus of control, learned helplessness or optimism, and subjective well-being. Parents can even influence largely inherited traits such as sensation seeking, and the authors suggest that uncaring, punitive parents could stifle inherited tendencies toward extraversion, sociability, agreeableness and openness.

Parenting style has been studied extensively. Children of authoritative parents, who are warm but firm, are more competent and mature than children of permissive, harsh or indifferent parents. Steinberg and Morris concluded that the combination of parental responsiveness and demandingness is consistently linked to adolescent adjustment, school performance and psychosocial maturity. In Singapore, adolescents with authoritative parents had more confidence in their abilities and better social adjustment than those with authoritarian parents, that is, strict, harsh and obedience-demanding (Ang). Parents' own personalities matter: parents high in extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness and openness behaved more warmly and consistently, and parents higher in agreeableness and lower in neuroticism supported their children's independence more (Prinzie and colleagues). Parents also play a major part in teaching children to be kind, caring and helpful (Fortuna and Knafo).

Parenting style varies with culture. Arab parents tend to be more authoritarian than authoritative, and immigrant mothers in Canada from collectivist cultures such as Egypt, Iran, India and Pakistan were more authoritarian than mothers from individualistic Western European countries (Rudy and Grusec).

Positive parental behaviour has positive effects: praise can promote autonomy, realistic standards, competence, self-efficacy and intrinsic motivation. Negative behaviour has harmful effects. Depressed and anxious adults tended to have had more rejecting, abusive, less caring parents (Brewin, Andrews and Gotlib). Mothers high in negative emotion and disagreeableness had children with more defiance, anger and disobedience (Kochanska and colleagues). In a 12-year Finnish study, mothers with hostile child-rearing attitudes when children were 3 and 6 had children who were hostile by 15 (Raikkonen and colleagues). A US study found that restrictive, cold, strict parenting at age 5 produced adults at 31 high in conformity and low in self-direction (Kasser, Koestner and Lekes).

Finally, what determines how parents behave? It was long assumed that parents simply copy their own upbringing. A study of more than 20,000 families from Australia to Japan to the United States found that genetic factors accounted for up to 40 percent of parental behaviour, and that some parental behaviour responds to the child's own behaviour (Klahr and Burt). Parents both influence and reflect their children's behaviour.
sections.simple: Almost every theorist after Freud agreed parents matter, though each stressed something different: rejection (Adler), warmth (Horney), the mother bond (Allport, Erikson), basic needs (Maslow) or unconditional positive regard (Rogers). Warm-but-firm authoritative parenting produces the most competent children, while cold, hostile or rejecting parenting is linked to later problems. Parents' behaviour is itself partly genetic and partly a reaction to the child.
keyPoints: Freud first stressed parents; Adler, Horney, Allport, Cattell, Erikson, Maslow and Rogers all echoed him with different emphases.
Authoritative (warm but firm) parenting beats permissive, harsh, indifferent or authoritarian parenting for competence and adjustment.
Parents' own Big Five traits predict warmth, consistency and support for independence.
Collectivist and Arab cultures tend toward more authoritarian parenting.
Rejecting, hostile or cold parenting predicts adult depression, anxiety, hostility and conformity.
Up to 40 percent of parental behaviour is genetic, and parents also react to their children (Klahr and Burt).

sections.heading: The Parental Factor: Other Caregivers and the Peer Controversy
sections.detailed:
The chapter next asks what happens when parents are not the only or main caregivers, for example when they share child care with day-care workers, friends or relatives while working outside the home. In a national longitudinal survey of children aged 3 to 12, no significant behaviour or self-esteem problems were found when mothers worked outside the home, and the researcher concluded that care by someone other than the mother had no negative effect on the variables studied (Harvey).

The kibbutzim of Israel provide a natural laboratory for surrogate caregiving. On these communal settlements mothers care for infants only in the first few months; after that, professional caregivers take primary responsibility, and children usually spend more time with these surrogate parents than with their own. Overall, kibbutz children functioned and adapted well, provided they had formed a secure relationship with their parents in infancy. The strength of that early bond was the best predictor of children becoming dominant, independent and achievement oriented. However, barracks-style communal sleeping in early childhood could lead to a more anxious, restrained and emotionally flat personality, and adults who had failed to bond with parents or caregivers showed introversion, less capacity for friendship and reduced emotional intensity in relationships (Aviezer and colleagues).

A major controversy arose in the late 1990s with the claim that parental behaviour has no long-term effect on a child's personality outside the home. According to this view, associated with Harris, peers matter far more than parents: children adopt the behaviours, attitudes and values of classmates and friends to win their approval. Supporters do not deny that parents influence children; they deny that this influence carries over outside the home. In Harris' vivid image, children shed home-learned behaviour when they go out, like discarding an unwanted sweater their mother made them wear.

Modest support came from a twin study in late adolescence: twins with more friends in common were more alike in personality than twins with fewer shared friends, suggesting friends had more impact than the home environment (Loehlin). Researchers who emphasise genetic factors also tend to minimise the parental effect, arguing that family environment contributes little to personality.

The chapter therefore presents a genuine disagreement: classic theorists from Freud onward and much parenting research stress parents, while the peer view and genetic researchers downplay them. The authors suggest that, however this is eventually resolved, whether by parents, peers, genes or a combination, it raises a further question: is personality fixed by these early influences, or can it change later? That question introduces the developmental factor.
sections.simple: Children of working mothers showed no problems with behaviour or self-esteem, and kibbutz children raised mostly by professional caregivers did well if they had a secure early bond with their parents. A late-1990s controversy (Harris) claimed peers shape personality outside the home far more than parents do, with some twin support. Genetic researchers also play down parents' role.
keyPoints: Harvey: children aged 3 to 12 with working mothers showed no significant behaviour or self-esteem problems.
Kibbutz children adapted well if they had a secure early bond with parents; that bond best predicted dominance, independence and achievement.
Communal sleeping and failure to bond were linked to anxiety, emotional flatness, introversion and weaker friendships.
Harris: parental influence is specific to the home; peers shape personality outside it.
Loehlin: twins sharing more friends were more alike, modestly supporting the peer view; genetic researchers also minimise parental effects.

sections.heading: The Developmental Factor: Stability and Change Across the Life Span
sections.detailed:
Freud held that personality is shaped and fixed by about age 5 and is hard to change afterwards. Later research agrees that childhood is crucial but shows that personality continues developing well beyond childhood, possibly across the whole life span. Cattell, Allport and Erikson saw childhood as important but agreed that personality can be modified later. Some theorists stressed continuing development in adolescence, while Jung, Maslow, Erikson and Cattell treated middle age as a time of major personality change. This makes the developmental factor a clear point of disagreement between Freud and most later theorists.

How long does personality keep changing, and does personality at 20 predict personality at 40? The authors call this a highly complex question and perhaps not the right one. Evidence supports both change and stability. The better-framed question is whether some characteristics stay stable while others change, and to that the answer is an unqualified yes.

Research suggests that a basic foundation of enduring dispositions, such as McCrae and Costa's five factors, remains stable over many years, appearing enduring from age 30 onward (Nave and colleagues; Terracciano, McCrae and Costa). Some studies show neuroticism, extraversion and openness declining from college age to middle age while agreeableness and conscientiousness rise, a pattern found in countries as diverse as the United States, Germany, Italy, Portugal, Croatia, the Netherlands, Australia and South Korea (Allemand and colleagues; McCrae and Costa; Lucas and Donnellan).

Other results differ. A 40-year study found dominance and independence peaking in middle age, with personality still evolving after 20 (Helson, Jones and Kwan). A meta-analysis of 152 longitudinal studies with more than 55,000 people found high trait consistency at all ages, greatest in adulthood and highest after age 50 (Roberts and Delvecchio).

For childhood and adolescence, Estonian teenagers aged 12 to 18 stayed stable on the five factors over two years (Pullmann and colleagues), whereas American college students became more open, agreeable and conscientious over 30 months (Vaidya and colleagues). Normal and abnormal personality factors may reach peak stability around 30 and stay fairly stable afterward (Ferguson). Yet in Switzerland people in their 60s became less neurotic, less extraverted and less open (Allemand, Zimprich and Martin), and twins aged 64 to 98 showed declining extraversion, conscientiousness and perceived control with some rise in neuroticism, but no significant change in well-being (Berg and Johansson; Kandler and colleagues).

An Internet study of over 32,000 people aged 21 to 60 found conscientiousness and agreeableness increasing through early and middle adulthood, conscientiousness most in the 20s and agreeableness most in the 30s (Srivastava and colleagues). People also become more socially dominant, conscientious and emotionally stable from young adulthood to middle age (Roberts, Walton and Viechtbauer), and large-scale studies support general stability after 30 into late adulthood (Johnson and colleagues; Terracciano and colleagues). New Zealanders aged 18 to 26 showed growing psychological maturity: more self-control and social confidence, less anger and alienation, with women more mature overall (Roberts, Caspi and Moffitt). Children surveyed at 8 to 12 and again 10 years later showed that their changes between 18 and 22 were predictable from childhood personality (Shiner, Masten and Tellegen). Together these studies confirm that personality changes through adolescence and early adulthood.
sections.simple: Freud thought personality was set by age 5, but most later theorists and the research disagree. Basic traits like the Big Five become fairly stable around age 30, yet people still change: they tend to become more agreeable, conscientious and emotionally stable as they mature. So some parts of personality stay stable while others keep changing.
keyPoints: Freud: personality fixed by about age 5; Cattell, Allport and Erikson: childhood important but personality modifiable later.
Jung, Maslow, Erikson and Cattell saw middle age as a period of major change.
Best answer: some characteristics stay stable while others change.
Big Five traits appear stable from about age 30; N, E and O tend to decline and A and C to rise with age across many countries.
Roberts and Delvecchio: trait consistency rises with age, peaking after 50; Helson: dominance and independence peak in middle age.
Adolescence and early adulthood bring growing maturity, predictable partly from childhood personality.

sections.heading: The Developmental Factor: Why Adults Change and McAdams' Three Levels
sections.detailed:
If personality keeps changing in adulthood, what causes the change? Many psychologists locate the answer in social and environmental influences and in how we adapt to them. Changing economic circumstances, leaving college, marriage and parenthood, divorce, job loss or promotion, midlife crises and ageing parents all create problems adults must adjust to (McAdams and Olson).

Research supports this adaptation view. A 3-year Dutch study of people in their 40s found that those who had adapted successfully to expected social roles, such as career and family success, scored higher on the five-factor dimensions than those who had not, so personality change was tied to successful adaptation to midlife concerns (Van Aken and colleagues). People who lost their jobs showed significant increases in neuroticism and decreases in conscientiousness and extraversion. Adults who were actively dating and maintaining social relationships scored lower in neuroticism and higher in extraversion, conscientiousness and self-esteem than those who were not (Costa and colleagues; Neyer and Asendorpf). Such cultural and personal challenges leave their mark on personality.

To reconcile stability and change, McAdams proposed that personality develops over time on three levels. The first is dispositional traits: inherited traits of the kind McCrae and Costa described, which remain stable and relatively unchanging from about age 30. The second is personal concerns: our conscious feelings, plans and goals, what we want, how we try to get it, and how we feel about the people in our lives. These may change often across life because we meet so many different situations; yet the underlying traits we bring to those situations, such as our basic neuroticism or extraversion, can stay much the same. The third is the life narrative: shaping the self, achieving an identity and finding a unified purpose. We are continually writing our life story, creating who we are and how we fit into the world. Like personal concerns, the narrative changes with social and environmental circumstances, and adults revise it to fit each life stage and its needs, challenges and opportunities.

In sum, McAdams' view holds that underlying dispositional traits stay largely constant, while our conscious judgements about who we are and who we want to be remain open to change. This resolves the apparent contradiction in the research, and its focus on conscious judgements leads naturally to the next factor, consciousness.
sections.simple: Adults change mainly because they have to adapt to life events like marriage, parenthood, divorce, job loss or midlife challenges; adapting well is linked to healthier personality scores. McAdams said personality has three levels: stable inherited traits, changeable personal goals and plans, and a life story we keep rewriting.
keyPoints: Adult change is rooted in adapting to life events such as marriage, parenthood, divorce, job changes and ageing parents (McAdams and Olson).
Van Aken: successful adaptation to midlife roles was linked to higher five-factor scores.
Job loss raises neuroticism and lowers conscientiousness and extraversion; active dating and social ties show the opposite pattern.
McAdams' three levels: dispositional traits (stable from about 30), personal concerns (changeable goals and plans), life narrative (evolving life story).
Underlying traits stay constant while conscious self-judgements change.

sections.heading: The Consciousness Factor
sections.detailed:
Nearly every personality theory in the book deals, openly or implicitly, with conscious or cognitive processes. This is one of the clearest areas of agreement among the theorists.

Even Freud and Jung, who concentrated on the unconscious, described an ego or conscious mind that perceives, thinks, feels and remembers, allowing us to deal with the real world. Through the ego we perceive stimuli and later recall images of them. Jung also wrote about rational functioning, the making of conscious judgements and evaluations of our experiences. Adler portrayed people as conscious, rational beings able to plan and direct their lives; we form hopes, plans and dreams, delay gratification and consciously anticipate the future.

Allport believed that non-neurotic people function consciously and rationally, aware of and in control of what motivates them. Rogers saw people as primarily rational beings governed by their conscious perception of themselves and their experience. Maslow recognised consciousness in proposing cognitive needs to know and to understand.

Kelly offered the most complete cognitively based theory. He argued that we form constructs about our environment and other people and use them to make predictions or anticipations. We frame hypotheses about our social world and test them against experience. The authors note that everyday evidence makes it hard to deny that people construe, predict and anticipate others' behaviour and adjust their own accordingly.

Bandura credited people with the ability to learn from examples and vicarious reinforcement. This requires us to anticipate and appreciate the consequences of the actions we observe in others; we imagine the reinforcement we would receive for imitating a model even if we have never experienced it ourselves, which is itself a conscious cognitive process.

The theorists differ in emphasis, from Freud and Jung, for whom consciousness is only part of the mind, to Kelly, for whom cognition is the whole theory. But the chapter concludes that there is widespread agreement that consciousness exists and influences personality. There is much less agreement about the role, or even the existence, of the unconscious.
sections.simple: Almost all theorists agree that conscious thinking shapes personality. Freud and Jung described the conscious ego, Adler, Allport and Rogers saw people as rational planners, Maslow proposed needs to know and understand, Kelly built a whole theory on how we predict the world, and Bandura showed we imagine the results of copying others.
keyPoints: Almost every theory deals with conscious (cognitive) processes; this is wide agreement.
Freud and Jung: the ego perceives, thinks, feels and remembers; Jung added rational functioning.
Adler, Allport and Rogers: people are conscious, rational beings who plan and direct their lives.
Maslow: cognitive needs to know and understand.
Kelly: most complete cognitive theory; constructs used to predict and anticipate events.
Bandura: learning through models requires anticipating consequences.

sections.heading: The Unconscious Factor
sections.detailed:
Sigmund Freud introduced psychology to the unconscious, which he pictured as a murky store of our darkest fears, conflicts and forces that affect conscious thought and behaviour. Psychologists have found some evidence supporting Freud's idea that thoughts and memories are repressed into the unconscious and that repression and other defence mechanisms may operate at an unconscious level.

The cognitive movement in psychology has sparked not only interest in conscious processes but also renewed interest in the unconscious. Recent research confirms that the unconscious is a powerful force, possibly even more pervasive than Freud believed. However, the modern picture differs from Freud's. Contemporary researchers study unconscious cognitive processes and describe them as more rational than emotional.

This rational unconscious is often called the non-conscious, to distinguish it from Freud's unconscious, his dark cauldron of repressed wishes and desires. One way to study the non-conscious is subliminal activation: stimuli are presented below the level of conscious awareness, and although participants cannot perceive them, the stimuli can still activate their conscious processes and behaviour. The obvious conclusion is that people can be influenced by stimuli they can neither see nor hear.

The chapter also recalls the 'Mommy and I are one' research, in which subliminal presentation of certain stimuli influenced cognitive as well as emotional responses and even had therapeutic value although participants were unaware of the messages (Silverman and Weinberger). This suggests the unconscious may have both a rational and an emotional component, so the modern view and Freud's view need not be entirely opposed.

There is clear disagreement among the theorists here. Although the unconscious is an active research topic today, many personality theorists who followed Freud ignored it altogether. The authors suggest that the emotional unconscious as Freud conceived it, the startling idea that marked the formal start of the study of personality, remains the least understood factor of all, still as mysterious and inaccessible as it was in Freud's time.
sections.simple: Freud's unconscious was a dark store of repressed fears and wishes, and there is some support for repression. Today researchers study a more rational 'non-conscious', for example through subliminal stimuli that affect us without our awareness. Many theorists after Freud ignored the unconscious, and Freud's emotional unconscious remains the least understood factor.
keyPoints: Freud: unconscious as a repository of fears, conflicts and repressed wishes; some evidence supports repression.
The cognitive movement renewed interest in the unconscious, now seen as powerful and possibly more pervasive than Freud thought.
Modern view: the non-conscious, a rational rather than emotional unconscious.
Subliminal activation shows stimuli below awareness can influence thought and behaviour.
'Mommy and I are one' study (Silverman and Weinberger): subliminal stimuli affected emotions and had therapeutic value.
Many later theorists ignored the unconscious; Freud's emotional unconscious remains the least understood factor.

sections.heading: Final Comment
sections.detailed:
The closing comment admits that, like the unconscious, most aspects of personality remain mysterious and some are still not fully accessible. The course has presented many different ways of defining and describing personality, and each theory has added another part of the answer to the central question of what personality is.

The authors trace the journey from Freud, with his emphasis on anxiety, the unconscious and a life of fear and repression, to positive psychology and the characteristics of the happy personality, with many ideas in between, all adding to our understanding. This contrast captures how much the field's view of human nature has shifted, from a pessimistic, conflict-driven picture to one focused on well-being.

The authors stress that the field is unfinished. There are more possibilities to consider and more to learn, and new approaches and theories not yet imagined will no doubt appear. Although a student's formal course may be ending, the attempt to understand personality is not. Enormous progress has been made in charting personality and the factors that shape it, but the challenges remain active and dynamic.

The chapter ends by suggesting that 'What is personality?' may be the most important question in all of psychology, because it represents the attempt to understand ourselves. For exam purposes, this conclusion supports a balanced, integrative stance: each theory is partial, each contributes, and the seven factors work together rather than in isolation.
sections.simple: Much about personality is still a mystery, but each theory has added part of the answer, from Freud's anxious, repressed view to positive psychology's happy personality. New theories will keep coming, and understanding personality really means trying to understand ourselves.

terms.definition: The theme that many personality traits or dimensions are inherited, supported by twin and cross-cultural research on trait systems such as the Big Five.
The chapter's principle that heredity gives us tendencies rather than certainties; whether they are realised depends on social and environmental conditions, especially in childhood.
McCrae and Costa's model of five inherited dimensions: neuroticism, extraversion, openness to experience, agreeableness and conscientiousness.
Three inherited temperaments: emotionality, activity and sociability.
Zuckerman's trait, described as primarily influenced by genetic factors, though parental behaviour can influence it.
The theme that social and environmental forces, which become more important from childhood into adulthood, shape personality throughout life.
A group born and reared in the same period; Twenge's comparison of 1950s and 1980s cohorts showed generation-based differences in anxiety and neuroticism.
An identity developed by members of minority groups alongside their ego identity as they adapt to two cultures; a strong ethnic identity was linked to higher self-esteem and well-being.
Western cultures tend to be individualistic and score higher on extraversion, sensation seeking and subjective well-being than Eastern cultures.
The theme that learning shapes virtually every aspect of behaviour and is the route through which environmental forces affect personality, even modifying inherited tendencies.
Bandura's idea that we learn by watching models.
Bandura's concept of learning from the consequences others receive, which requires anticipating the results we would get for behaving like the model.

The broader notion uniting self-efficacy, internal locus of control, absence of learned helplessness and optimism: the belief that one controls one's life; it is learned in childhood, largely through parents.
A learned condition involving a lack of control, the opposite of high self-efficacy and internal locus of control.
The theme, first emphasised by Freud and echoed by nearly all later theorists, that parents' behaviour shapes the child's personality.
Warm but firm child-rearing that combines responsiveness and demandingness; linked to more competent, mature and well-adjusted children.
Strict, harsh child-rearing that demands obedience; more common in collectivist and Arab cultures and linked to poorer confidence and social adjustment than authoritative parenting.
Israeli communal settlement where professional caregivers take primary responsibility for children after the first few months, providing a natural test of non-parental care.
The late-1990s claim that parental influence is specific to the home and that peers shape a child's personality outside it far more than parents do.
The question of whether personality is fixed in early life or continues to change; the chapter concludes that some characteristics remain stable while others change.
McAdams' first level of personality: inherited traits of the McCrae and Costa kind that remain stable and relatively unchanging from about age 30.
McAdams' second level: conscious feelings, plans and goals, what we want and how we pursue it, which may change often over the life span.
McAdams' third level: the evolving life story through which we shape the self, attain identity and find unified purpose; revised to fit each life stage.
The theme, accepted by nearly all theorists, that conscious cognitive processes such as perceiving, thinking, planning and anticipating influence personality.
Kelly's cognitive concept: the ways we interpret our environment and other people, used to predict and anticipate events and tested against experience.
Freud's murky repository of our darkest fears, conflicts and repressed wishes that affect conscious thought and behaviour.
The modern rational unconscious studied by cognitive researchers, named to distinguish it from Freud's emotional unconscious.
A method of studying the non-conscious by presenting stimuli below conscious awareness; such stimuli can still activate thought and behaviour.

people.name: Sigmund Freud
people.contribution: First to emphasise parental influence; held that personality is fixed by about age 5; introduced the emotional unconscious, which remains the least understood factor; also described the conscious ego.

people.name: Jung
people.contribution: Source of the extraversion dimension; described the ego and rational functioning (conscious judgements); saw middle age as a time of major personality change.

people.name: Adler
people.contribution: Stressed birth order as an environmental influence and the harm of parental rejection; saw people as conscious, rational planners.

people.name: Horney
people.contribution: Highlighted culture (German versus American neuroses), gender-based environments and female inferiority in male-dominated culture; stressed lack of parental warmth as undermining security.

people.name: Allport
people.contribution: Said genetics supplies the raw material that the social environment shapes; saw the mother-infant bond as the source of security; viewed personality as modifiable later; held that non-neurotic people function consciously and rationally.

people.name: Cattell
people.contribution: Proposed 16 factors, some more heritable than others but all affected by environment; saw infancy as the major formative period; viewed middle age as a time of major change.

people.name: Erikson
people.contribution: Eight innate psychosocial stages realised through the environment; first-year mother relationship vital for trust; personality modifiable, with major change in middle age.

people.name: Maslow
people.contribution: Self-actualization innate but promoted or inhibited by environment; parents must meet physiological and safety needs in the first two years; proposed cognitive needs to know and understand.

people.name: Rogers
people.contribution: Self-actualization innate but environmentally influenced; parents must provide unconditional positive regard; people are primarily rational beings guided by conscious self-perception.

people.name: Eysenck
people.contribution: Three inherited dimensions: psychoticism, neuroticism and extraversion.

people.name: McCrae and Costa
people.contribution: Five-factor model of inherited traits, found stable from about age 30.

people.name: Buss and Plomin
people.contribution: Three inherited temperaments: emotionality, activity and sociability.

people.name: Zuckerman
people.contribution: Sensation seeking, a trait primarily influenced by genetics.

people.name: Skinner
people.contribution: Showed how reinforcement, successive approximation and superstitious behaviour shape behaviour; saw personality as an accumulation of learned responses.

people.name: Bandura
people.contribution: Observational learning, vicarious reinforcement and self-efficacy; agreed with Skinner that genetics plays a limited role; learning by example requires conscious anticipation of consequences.

people.name: Rotter
people.contribution: Locus of control, a learned aspect of personality related to the broader notion of control.

people.name: Seligman
people.contribution: Learned helplessness and optimism versus pessimism; people who feel in control are optimistic.

people.name: Kelly
people.contribution: Offered the most complete cognitive theory: we form constructs and use them to predict and anticipate events.

people.name: Harris
people.contribution: Proposed in the late 1990s that parental influence stays in the home and peers shape personality outside it.

people.name: McAdams
people.contribution: Proposed three levels of personality development: dispositional traits, personal concerns and life narrative.

studies.title: Yamagata et al. (2006): twins in Canada, Germany and Japan
studies.finding: Supported a genetic basis for the five-factor model, which may reflect a heritage common to the human species.

studies.title: Shiner (2014): Big Five over 20 years
studies.finding: The Big Five became increasingly stable from childhood into adulthood.

studies.title: DeFruyt et al. (2006); Kandler et al. (2010): twins and siblings in Germany and Belgium
studies.finding: High trait stability through childhood, adolescence and young adulthood, reinforcing genetic influence.

studies.title: Allik, Realo and McCrae (2013) and others: 50 cultures
studies.finding: The Big Five appeared consistently in most nations, but less consistently in developing countries such as Ethiopia, Lebanon, Malaysia and Uganda.

studies.title: Larsson, Andershed and Lichtenstein (2006): Swedish adolescent twins
studies.finding: Strong genetic component in psychopathic personality prone to violent antisocial behaviour.

studies.title: Garcia et al. (2013): heritability of anxiety
studies.finding: Heritability of anxiety increased between ages 14 and 18.

studies.title: Genetics of everyday behaviours (US, Finland, French Canada, Sweden)
studies.finding: Genetic influences on sexual attitudes, eating in 2-year-olds, depression in bullied children and attitudes to music practice; identical twins more likely than fraternal twins to own guns.

studies.title: Briley and Tucker-Drob (2014); Kandler (2012): genes versus environment over age
studies.finding: Genetic effects are most important in infancy; environmental effects grow from childhood to adulthood and continue throughout life.

studies.title: Twenge (2000): 1950s versus 1980s birth cohorts
studies.finding: Among more than 50,000 students and young people, the 1980s cohort was substantially higher in anxiety and neuroticism, attributed to decreased social connectedness.

studies.title: Jokela et al. (2009): becoming a parent in Finland
studies.finding: Parenthood brought more stress and anxiety, lower marital and life satisfaction, and higher emotionality that rose with the number of children.

studies.title: Wendorf et al. (2011): parenthood in the US, England and Turkey
studies.finding: Parenthood lowered marital satisfaction; more children meant lower satisfaction.

studies.title: Roberts, Caspi and Moffitt (2003): jobs in New Zealand
studies.finding: Young adults with satisfying, high-status jobs at 26 increased in positive and decreased in negative emotionality since 18; the workplace can affect innate traits.

studies.title: Sutin et al. (2010): stressful life events
studies.finding: High-neuroticism people saw stressful events as negative turning points and became more neurotic; high-extraversion people saw lessons and became more extraverted.

studies.title: Usborne and Taylor (2010): ethnic identity in Canada
studies.finding: Minority members with the strongest ethnic identities had the highest self-esteem and subjective well-being.

studies.title: Rentfrow (2010): US regions
studies.finding: Neuroticism higher in northeastern and southeastern states, agreeableness higher in the south, extraversion higher in the northeast and lower in the west.

studies.title: Hart, Atkins and Matsuba (2008): disadvantaged neighbourhoods
studies.finding: Children from economically disadvantaged neighbourhoods more likely to show maladaptive tendencies, low resiliency and problem behaviours.

studies.title: Jokela et al. (2015): London neighbourhoods
studies.finding: Life satisfaction, agreeableness, conscientiousness and openness varied across neighbourhoods.

studies.title: Bleidorn et al. (2010): learning and life goals
studies.finding: Learning plays a major role in virtually every aspect of behaviour, including personality and major life goals.

studies.title: Steinberg and Morris (2001): authoritative parenting
studies.finding: Parental responsiveness combined with demandingness is consistently related to adolescent adjustment, school performance and psychosocial maturity.

studies.title: Ang (2006): Singapore adolescents
studies.finding: Adolescents with authoritative parents had more confidence and better social adjustment than those with authoritarian parents.

studies.title: Prinzie et al. (2009): parent personality
studies.finding: Parents high in E, A, C and O were warmer and more consistent; parents higher in agreeableness and lower in neuroticism supported independence more.

studies.title: Fortuna and Knafo (2014): kindness
studies.finding: Parents play a major role in teaching children to be kind, caring and helpful.

studies.title: Rudy and Grusec (2006): immigrant mothers in Canada
studies.finding: Mothers from collectivist cultures (Egypt, Iran, India, Pakistan) were more authoritarian than mothers from individualistic Western Europe.

studies.title: Brewin, Andrews and Gotlib (1993): childhood and adult psychopathology
studies.finding: Depressed and anxious adults had parents who were more rejecting and abusive and less caring and affectionate.

studies.title: Kochanska, Clark and Goldman (1997): maternal negativity
studies.finding: Mothers high in negative emotion and disagreeableness had children with more defiance, anger, disobedience and behaviour problems.

studies.title: Raikkonen et al. (2000): 12-year Finnish study
studies.finding: Mothers with hostile child-rearing attitudes when children were 3 and 6 had children who were hostile at 15.

studies.title: Kasser, Koestner and Lekes (2002): ages 5 to 31
studies.finding: Restrictive, cold, strict parenting at 5 produced adults high in conformity and low in self-direction.

studies.title: Klahr and Burt (2014): over 20,000 families
studies.finding: Genetic factors accounted for up to 40 percent of parental behaviour, and some parental behaviour responds to the child's behaviour.

studies.title: Harvey (1999): working mothers
studies.finding: Children aged 3 to 12 showed no significant behaviour or self-esteem problems when mothers worked outside the home.

studies.title: Aviezer et al. (1994): kibbutz child rearing
studies.finding: Kibbutz children adapted well if securely bonded with parents in infancy; communal sleeping and failure to bond were linked to anxiety, emotional flatness, introversion and weaker friendships.

studies.title: Loehlin (1997): twins and shared friends
studies.finding: Twins with more friends in common were more alike in personality, modestly supporting peer over home influence.

studies.title: Nave et al. (2010); Terracciano, McCrae and Costa (2010): stability after 30
studies.finding: Basic traits and capacities appear enduring from age 30 onward.

studies.title: Allemand et al. (2008); McCrae and Costa (1997) and others: cross-cultural age trends
studies.finding: Neuroticism, extraversion and openness decline and agreeableness and conscientiousness increase from college to middle age in many countries.

studies.title: Helson, Jones and Kwan (2002): 40-year study
studies.finding: Dominance and independence peaked in middle age; personality kept changing after 20.

studies.title: Roberts and Delvecchio (2000): meta-analysis of 152 studies
studies.finding: High trait consistency at all ages, greatest in adulthood and highest after age 50.

studies.title: Pullmann, Raudsepp and Allik (2006): Estonian teens
studies.finding: Five-factor personality of 12- to 18-year-olds stayed stable over two years.

studies.title: Vaidya et al. (2002): American college students
studies.finding: Students became more open, agreeable and conscientious over 30 months.

studies.title: Ferguson (2010): peak stability
studies.finding: Normal and abnormal personality factors may reach peak stability around 30 and stay fairly stable.

studies.title: Allemand, Zimprich and Martin (2008): Swiss people in their 60s
studies.finding: Became less neurotic, less extraverted and less open with age.

studies.title: Berg and Johansson (2014); Kandler et al. (2014): twins aged 64 to 98
studies.finding: Extraversion, conscientiousness and perceived control declined, neuroticism showed some increase, but well-being did not change significantly.

studies.title: Srivastava et al. (2003): Internet study of 32,000 adults
studies.finding: Conscientiousness and agreeableness increased through early and middle adulthood, conscientiousness most in the 20s and agreeableness most in the 30s.

studies.title: Roberts, Walton and Viechtbauer (2006): young to middle adulthood
studies.finding: People become more socially dominant, conscientious and emotionally stable.

studies.title: Johnson et al. (2005); Terracciano et al. (2006): large-scale stability studies
studies.finding: Personality remains generally stable after 30 into late adulthood.

studies.title: Roberts, Caspi and Moffitt (2001): New Zealand ages 18 to 26
studies.finding: Increasing psychological maturity: more self-control and social confidence, less anger and alienation; women more mature overall.

studies.title: Shiner, Masten and Tellegen (2002): childhood predicts change
studies.finding: Personality change between 18 and 22 could be predicted from personality at ages 8 to 12.

studies.title: Van Aken et al. (2006): Dutch adults in their 40s
studies.finding: Those who adapted successfully to expected social roles scored higher on five-factor dimensions.

studies.title: Costa et al. (2000); Neyer and Asendorpf (2001): job loss and dating
studies.finding: Job loss increased neuroticism and decreased conscientiousness and extraversion; active daters were lower in neuroticism and higher in extraversion, conscientiousness and self-esteem.

studies.finding: Subliminal stimuli influenced cognitive and emotional responses and had therapeutic value without conscious awareness.

examples.title: Predisposition, not destiny
examples.text: Two cousins both seem naturally outgoing as toddlers. One grows up in a lively joint family where talking to guests is praised; the other has strict, punitive parents who scold every outburst. By college the first is the class organiser and the second is quiet and guarded. The inherited tendency was similar; the environment decided how far it was expressed.

examples.title: Authoritative versus authoritarian at exam time
examples.text: An authoritative parent says: 'Board exams matter, so let's fix a study timetable together, and you can still play cricket on Sunday.' An authoritarian parent says: 'No phone, no cricket, study because I said so.' Both are demanding, but only the first combines demandingness with warmth and responsiveness.

examples.title: Peers outside the home
examples.text: A boy speaks his mother tongue and is very polite at home, but at school he copies the slang, music and attitude of his friends to fit in. On Harris' view, the home behaviour stays at home and the peer group shapes the personality he shows outside.

examples.title: McAdams' three levels in one person
examples.text: A woman has been anxious and introverted all her adult life (dispositional trait). At 25 her goal was a government job; at 35 it is starting a small bakery (personal concern). Over time her story about herself shifts from 'I play it safe' to 'I took a risk and built something' (life narrative). The trait stays; the goals and story change.

examples.title: Subliminal influence
examples.text: Imagine a word flashed on a screen too fast to be seen, and participants afterwards answer questions differently even though none of them report seeing anything. This is the logic of subliminal activation: the non-conscious registers what consciousness misses.
